title: I Took the Planer-Bed Reservation to the Chair Who Left My Knives

parts.text: I stepped into planer bay at 8:06 a.m. and chair Reed was already using my numbered knives. The board said: FORTY MINUTES. KNIVES STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty-six, mill steward, holding a clipboard that listed our thickness. Reed shrugged. "Chairs keep the bed." I photographed the board, the booking, and his stock on my knives. Then I asked for the bed reservation. At 8:14 the mill desk pinged why Reed's stock sat on our knives. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The mill desk can see Reed's stock on the planer during our thickness.

social.video_title: He left his stock on my numbered knives — Part 1/2
social.description: Planer bay, a chair on my knives, a forty-minute clock he posted. I logged the stock. Would you have asked for the bed reservation?

parts.text: Reed called it snipe tests until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the bed still. The knives went back to my numbered case. Reed ran a slot of their own and told the next chair atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: CHAIRS DO NOT KEEP THE BED. I keep our thickness on a labeled card. Reed brown-bags his stock. The planer finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Chairs do not keep the bed — Part 2/2
social.description: Bed reservation, numbered knives, and a second line on the board. Were snipe tests ever our thickness?
